title: The elevator
hookLine: Thérèse, too small to climb the stairs of perfection, looks for a lift: Jesus's arms

lines: A STEEP STAIRCASE, A SMALL CHILD.
SAINTS LIKE MOUNTAINS, SHE LIKE SAND.
cards: A steep, rough staircase, and at the bottom someone very small, looking up at it. That's the picture a young French Carmelite, Thérèse of Lisieux, used for herself when she looked at the saints.
They seemed to her like mountains, and she like a grain of sand. She could have given up there, or gritted her teeth and climbed harder. Thérèse did neither.
She went looking for a machine. You met it briefly on day ninety-three; today, how she built it.

teach.h: AN AGE OF INVENTIONS: A LIFT.
teach.b: In the pages later published as Story of a Soul, Thérèse writes that she lives in an age of inventions.
In wealthy homes, people no longer bother with the stairs: a lift carries them up. She wants one too, a lift to Jesus, because she is too little to climb the rough stairway of perfection.
So she goes looking in Scripture, and she finds two lines. The first is from Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me."
The second is from the end of Isaiah, God speaking as a mother: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you."

teach.h: SCRIPTURE: THE LITTLE ONES ARE CARRIED.
teach.b: Isaiah adds that the little ones will be carried and dandled on the knees. Then comes her conclusion, the turn the whole image is built for.
The elevator, she says, is your arms, Jesus. And for that, she doesn't need to grow up.

teach.h: WHOSOEVER IS A LITTLE ONE, LET HIM COME TO ME.
teach.b: She needs to stay little, and become more so. That's the heart of what she called her little way. Notice what it isn't.
It isn't laziness: Thérèse worked hard and kept a demanding Rule. It isn't pretending to be helpless. It's a change in who does the lifting.

Effort stays, but the anxious grading of your own spiritual height goes. Jesus says something close in Matthew: "unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven."
The little way might sound like this: I can't climb this by myself. I'll keep taking the small steps, and let myself be carried.

how: Catholics who follow Thérèse's little way read Story of a Soul and try to bring small daily acts to God with childlike trust, rather than measuring their own spiritual progress.

o: a quick shortcut to holiness that skips all effort
Thérèse's image of being carried up to God by Jesus

games.q: you're Thérèse. the saints look like mountains, and you feel like a grain of sand at the foot of a steep staircase. what do you do?
o: grit your teeth and climb harder.
look for a lift, and find it in the arms of Jesus.
games.why: she searches Scripture, finds the little ones carried, and concludes: the elevator is your arms, Jesus. she needs to stay little.

practice: Name one thing you've been trying to climb on your own, a habit, a worry, a standard you can't meet, and picture it as that staircase.
If you pray, tell Jesus plainly that it's too high for you, and ask to be carried; if you don't, picture setting it down in the arms of someone who loves you, and notice what your shoulders do.

wordCard.voice: The elevator. Thérèse's image for the little way: too small for the stairs, she is lifted up in the arms of Jesus. Today's word.

orig.note: French, Thérèse's own word: elevator, a lift.

carryVoice: Your line: carried up. The small steps still count, but the lifting isn't all yours. Rest well.
